title: Job Search and Employment Readiness in Canada
summary: By the end, learners can search for jobs on Job Bank, describe what belongs in a resume and a cover letter, tailor an application to one posting, use a Job Bank account with care, and prepare for an interview using official Canadian and Alberta tips.
goals: By the end, learners can search for jobs on Job Bank, describe what belongs in a resume and a cover letter, tailor an application to one posting, use a Job Bank account with care, and prepare for an interview using official Canadian and Alberta tips.
certificateNote: It is not a college diploma, degree, trade ticket, professional licence, guaranteed job, or legal, immigration, or Employment Insurance advice.

lessons.title: Where to look for work
lessons.html:
A job search means looking for work in an organized way. The Government of Canada’s Job Bank is a free official website where you can browse thousands of jobs across Canada. On Job Bank you can narrow results with filters such as hours of work, benefits, and salary. You can also sign up for Job Alerts, a free email service that sends new postings, and search on the Job Bank mobile app.

Job Bank also says you can look beyond one website: attend job fairs (online or in person), contact recruiters, and use social media to grow your work network.

In Alberta, alis (Alberta’s official careers and work-search site) has a “Look for Work” section with articles on work-search basics, resumes, and how to apply. If you want to talk to someone, alis lists the Alberta Supports Contact Centre at 1-877-644-9992 (toll free).

A simple start:

  1. Open Job Bank’s find-a-job page.
  2. Type a job title or skill and a place, such as your town or a nearby city.
  3. Use filters if the list is long.
  4. Read the full posting before you apply.
  5. Write down the closing date and how to apply.

This course cannot guarantee you a job. It also will not tell you about work permits, immigration categories, or EI. Job Bank has a separate area for people outside Canada; use official pages or settlement staff for those questions.

Ask your adult learning council if they run employment-readiness workshops.

lessons.title: Build a resume that matches the job
lessons.html:
A resume (alis often writes resumé) tells an employer who you are and what you can do. Job Bank says a good resume shows your background, skills, and qualifications, and that you should tailor it to the job by highlighting relevant accomplishments.

Alis suggests starting with a master resume — one long list of your contact information, education and training, work history (most recent job first), skills, accomplishments, volunteer work, awards, and references. Update it often. Then copy the most useful parts into a shorter resume for each job.

Alis describes three common layouts:

  • Chronological — work and education from newest to oldest. Helpful when the job is similar to work you have done.
  • Functional — focuses on skills. May help if you have gaps in paid work.
  • Combination — skills first, then a short work history. Useful if you are changing fields.

Official tips that help:

  • Study the posting and use the same keywords the employer used (alis notes that some software screens resumes for those words).
  • Keep the version you send short — alis says 1 to 2 pages at most.
  • Use a simple, easy-to-read font and point form. Alis says to avoid tables or columns because some screening software cannot read them well.
  • Submit a Word file (.doc or .docx) if the posting allows it; alis says some screening software cannot read PDF files.
  • Be honest. Proofread out loud, use spell check carefully (it may not know cheque from check), and ask a trusted person to read it.

Job Bank has a free Resume Builder after you sign in. It currently describes a traditional template and a template for youth or recent graduates. You fill in the blanks and can save more than one resume.

lessons.title: Research, cover letters, and how to apply
lessons.html:
Job Bank says applying for a job involves three steps: research the company or job, create a resume, and prepare a cover letter.

Research first. Before you send anything, try to learn:

  • What the company does
  • The duties of the job
  • The qualifications and skills required
  • Who the customers or clients are
  • What reputation the employer has

Job Bank says this research helps you write the resume and cover letter and prepare for an interview. You can use the posting, the company’s website, and (if it feels safe) people who work in that field.

A cover letter is your introduction. Job Bank says it should be concise, well written, and tailored to that company and job. You may need a different letter for each job. It should give the employer an idea of who you are and highlight the skills you offer.

On its “stand out” page, Job Bank suggests:

  • a short opening that shows interest
  • your top skills that match the posting, with one or two clear examples
  • a closing that repeats your interest or thanks the reader

A cover letter is not always required, but when it is, Job Bank says taking time to write a good one can make a real difference.

When you apply: follow the instructions on the posting exactly (email, website form, or in person). Attach the files they ask for. Keep a copy of what you sent and the date.

If a posting feels like a scam (for example, it asks for a banking password or a fee to “guarantee” a job), stop and ask council staff. See also the LearnHere email-safety course.

lessons.title: Job Bank accounts and applying online
lessons.html:
You can browse many Job Bank postings without extra tools. If you want to save searches and get alerts, Job Bank offers free accounts.

A Standard account, according to Job Bank’s find-a-job page, can be started with an email address. With it you can customize searches, get daily Job Alerts, and use resume templates to prepare an application.

A Plus account adds more tools, such as matching you with openings from a profile, invitations from employers, and applying from some postings with a saved resume or one made in the Resume Builder.

Some extra services, including Job Match and Direct Apply, ask you to confirm that you are a Canadian citizen, a permanent resident, or a temporary resident. To prove eligibility, Job Bank may ask for your date of birth, a parent’s last name at birth, and your valid Social Insurance Number (SIN). Job Bank says the SIN is checked automatically and will not be kept in its records.

Important: If you cannot provide that information or prefer not to, Job Bank says you can still sign up by opting out of those extra services. You can add the information later if you change your mind. This course will not tell you which immigration category you are in, and you should not type your SIN into this course.

When a posting offers Direct Apply, follow the official steps on Job Bank and read any box that asks you to share your email and documents with that employer.

Keep your Job Bank password private, just as you would for email.

lessons.title: Prepare for the interview
lessons.html:
An interview is a meeting where an employer asks about your skills and you learn about the job. Being invited is already a step forward. This course cannot promise the job.

Job Bank says to prepare in advance:

  • Research the company.
  • Think of questions they might ask and prepare answers from your work or education.
  • Use the STAR method to structure examples: Situation, Task, Action, Result.
  • Practise with friends or family.
  • On the day, bring copies of your resume and a list of references, and dress in a way that fits the workplace.

Alis uses a similar method called STARS (Situation, Task, Action, Result, Skills) and offers four habits:

  1. Prepare — learn about the company and the job; review your resume; plan examples; prepare questions to ask them; bring a reference list. Alis also says to understand your rights about what kinds of questions are appropriate. This course is not legal advice; ask council staff or official resources if a question worries you.
  2. Practise — say answers out loud; try a practice interview with a friend.
  3. Present yourself well — be neat and on time; turn off your cellphone.
  4. Participate — listen carefully; answer thoughtfully; you may take notes. Afterward, alis suggests a short thank-you note or email that names two or three reasons you are a good fit.

If you want more help in Alberta, call the Alberta Supports Contact Centre at 1-877-644-9992, or ask your adult learning council about interview practice.
